details.exam_pattern: Predictability is Medium-High. The recent format is strong evidence, but it does not cover the whole current syllabus and earlier papers differ.
details.title: MA4344 - Advanced Group Theory
exam_block: Q1: matrix subgroup of SL(2,Z) isomorphic to Z , then Lagrange's theorem / isomorphism theorem / homomorphism consequences.
Q2: cosets, left/right index equality, index 2 normal subgroup, then simple groups or centre/quotient arguments.
Q3: group actions embedded into a symmetric group, then class equation, nontrivial centre of p-groups, and groups of order p^2 being abelian.
Q4: Cauchy's theorem for finite abelian groups, Sylow's theorem, then proving specific group orders are not simple.
drill: Recent papers are very similar, especially 2023/24 and 2024/25.
Core repeat areas: Lagrange's theorem, isomorphism theorems, homomorphism image/order arguments, cosets and normal subgroups.
Group actions recur strongly: kernels, stabilisers, embeddings into symmetric groups, orbits and conjugacy-style arguments.
Class equation and p-group results are high-value: nontrivial centre and groups of order p^2 being abelian.
Cauchy's theorem, finite abelian groups, Sylow theorems and proving groups are not simple are central preparation targets.

Older papers add direct products, alternating groups, automorphisms, Euclidean/wallpaper groups and Burnside counting; useful background, but the newest pattern is more focused on cosets, actions, class equation and Sylow.

cards.front: Cauchy's theorem, exponent, direct product, finite abelian group. The finite-abelian theorem: if p divides |G|
cards.back: If prime p divides |G|, Cauchy gives an element of order p. A finite abelian group decomposes as a direct product of cyclic prime-power groups, uniquely up to order.

cards.back: |G|=|Z(G)|+sum [G:C_G(x_i)]; noncentral conjugacy-class sizes divide |G| and exceed 1; a finite p-group has nontrivial centre.

sheets.title: Cauchy's Theorem and Finite Abelian Groups
sheets.purpose: State and prove the finite-abelian version of Cauchy's theorem, and use it in order arguments. Exam use: Prime factorisation, theorem hypotheses, complete partition list and an isomorphism invariant are visible.

practice.title: Practice 1 — classify abelian groups of order 72 [10 marks]
practice.prompt: Classify all finite abelian groups of order 72 up to isomorphism, then distinguish a cyclic and a non-cyclic example.
practice.route: This is a prime-power decomposition and counting problem, not a request to list divisors. Fastest route. Split 72=2³3², list partitions for each primary part, then combine them. Topic-specific trap. Coprime cyclic factors combine to a cyclic product, but an elementary abelian p-part does not become cyclic. Split 72=2³3², list partitions for each primary part, then combine them. Topic-specific trap. Coprime cyclic factors combine to a cyclic product, but an elementary abelian p-part does not become cyclic. Coprime cyclic factors combine to a cyclic product, but an elementary abelian p-part does not become cyclic.
practice.answer: Classify abelian groups of order 72=2^3*3^2. The 2-part is Z8, Z4xZ2, or Z2^3; the 3-part is Z9 or Z3^2. Combining independently gives 3*2=6 isomorphism types. For example Z8xZ9 is cyclic Z72, whereas Z2^3xZ3^2 has exponent lcm(2,3)=6, so they are not isomorphic.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. What does Cauchy's theorem give for an abelian group of order 40? Check: elements of orders 2 and 5 exist.
practice.route: 2. Explain why the quotient step in the induction proof is legal. Check: every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.
practice.answer: 2. Explain why the quotient step in the induction proof is legal. Check: every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.

practice.title: Practice 2 — square-free finite abelian groups [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Prove that every finite abelian group of square-free order n is cyclic.
practice.route: The proof must construct an element of order n. Fastest route. Use Cauchy for each prime factor and combine commuting elements of coprime orders. Topic-specific trap. The product-order argument needs both commutativity and coprime component orders. Use Cauchy for each prime factor and combine commuting elements of coprime orders. Topic-specific trap. The product-order argument needs both commutativity and coprime component orders. The product-order argument needs both commutativity and coprime component orders.
practice.answer: prove an abelian group of square-free order n is cyclic. Check Cauchy gives elements of each prime order; their product has order the product because the group is abelian and orders are coprime, hence order n.

mistakes: Claiming Cauchy gives an element of every divisor order.
Forgetting the finite hypothesis.
Confusing an element of order p with a subgroup of order p without linking them.
Recovery rule: Cauchy guarantees an element of order p, not automatically one of order p^a.

sheets.title: Class Equation and p-Groups
sheets.purpose: Prove the nontrivial-centre theorem and quickly derive the order-p² abelian result. Exam use: Centre term, representatives, centralizers, divisibility/mod-p step and final group consequence are justified.

practice.title: Practice 1 — groups of order p² [9 marks]
practice.prompt: Prove that a group G of order p² is abelian using the centre of a p-group.
practice.route: The centre-size cases must both be exhausted. Fastest route. Use p∣|Z(G)|; if |Z(G)|=p, show G/Z(G) is cyclic and invoke the cyclic-quotient lemma. Topic-specific trap. A cyclic quotient alone is not a conclusion unless the quotient is specifically by the centre. Use p∣|Z(G)|; if |Z(G)|=p, show G/Z(G) is cyclic and invoke the cyclic-quotient lemma. Topic-specific trap. A cyclic quotient alone is not a conclusion unless the quotient is specifically by the centre. A cyclic quotient alone is not a conclusion unless the quotient is specifically by the centre.
practice.answer: Let |G|=p^2. The p-group centre theorem gives |Z(G)| divisible by p and greater than 1, so |Z(G)| is p or p^2. If it were p, G/Z(G) would have order p and be cyclic. But if G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is abelian, forcing Z(G)=G, contradiction. Hence |Z(G)|=p^2 and G is abelian.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Why does a noncentral conjugacy class in a p-group have size divisible by p? Check: its size is a nontrivial power of p.
practice.route: 2. Prove that a group of order 49 is abelian. Check: apply the p² theorem with p=7.
practice.answer: 2. Prove that a group of order 49 is abelian. Check: apply the p² theorem with p=7.

practice.title: Practice 2 — possible noncentral conjugacy-class sizes [8 marks]
practice.prompt: If |G|=8 and |Z(G)|=2, determine the possible sizes of noncentral conjugacy classes and the resulting count constraint.
practice.route: This is an application of orbit-stabiliser to conjugation. Fastest route. Class sizes are [G:C G (x)], powers of 2 dividing 8, and are nonunit for noncentral x. Topic-specific trap. Do not count the identity again among the six noncentral elements. Class sizes are [G:C G (x)], powers of 2 dividing 8, and are nonunit for noncentral x. Topic-specific trap. Do not count the identity again among the six noncentral elements. Do not count the identity again among the six noncentral elements.
practice.answer: if |G|=8 and |Z(G)|=2, what can noncentral class sizes be? Check they are powers of 2 dividing 8 and cannot be 1; the six noncentral elements must partition into sizes 2 or 4, constrained by centralizer indices.

mistakes: Including central elements again in the noncentral sum.
Claiming every conjugacy class has p elements.
Using G/Z(G) cyclic without stating why that implies G abelian.
Recovery rule: The class equation sums one term per conjugacy class representative, not one term per noncentral element.

sheets.title: Cosets and Normal Subgroups
sheets.purpose: Prove left/right coset facts and deploy the high-yield index-2 normality argument. Exam use: Coset side, partition/count, normality criterion, counterexample element and quotient permission are explicit.

practice.title: Practice 1 — index two forces normality [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Prove that a subgroup H of index two in G is normal.
practice.route: The proof needs equality of left and right cosets for every g. Fastest route. Separate g∈H from g∉H and use uniqueness of the sole non-H coset. Topic-specific trap. A subgroup of another small index is not automatically normal. Separate g∈H from g∉H and use uniqueness of the sole non-H coset. Topic-specific trap. A subgroup of another small index is not automatically normal. A subgroup of another small index is not automatically normal.
practice.answer: Prove index 2 implies normal. There are exactly two left cosets: H and GH; likewise the right cosets are H and GH. For g in H, gH=H=Hg. For g notin H, both gH and Hg are the unique non-H coset GH. Hence gH=Hg for every g and H is normal.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. List the left cosets of 2Z in Z. Check: 2Z and 1+2Z.
practice.route: 2. Let H≤G and |G|=30, |H|=15. Prove H◃G and state |G/H|. Check: index 2; quotient has order 2.
practice.answer: 2. Let H≤G and |G|=30, |H|=15. Prove H◃G and state |G/H|. Check: index 2; quotient has order 2.

practice.title: Practice 2 — left/right cosets in S 3 [8 marks]
practice.prompt: For H={e,(12)}≤S 3 , list a contrasting left and right coset and decide normality.
practice.route: One explicit mismatch proves non-normality. Fastest route. Multiply (13) on the chosen side of both elements of H. Topic-specific trap. Preserve permutation-composition convention consistently when identifying (123) and (132). Multiply (13) on the chosen side of both elements of H. Topic-specific trap. Preserve permutation-composition convention consistently when identifying (123) and (132). Preserve permutation-composition convention consistently when identifying (123) and (132).
practice.answer: in S3 let H={<e>,(12)}. List left and right cosets and decide normality. Check (13)H={(13),(123)} while H(13)={(13),(132)}, so H is not normal despite having order 2.

mistakes: Treating left and right cosets as equal without normality.
Writing a quotient by a non-normal subgroup.
Assuming a subgroup of any small index is normal.
Recovery rule: A subgroup of order 2 need not be normal; the automatic theorem is index 2.

sheets.title: Group Actions
sheets.purpose: Construct action homomorphisms and use orbit-stabiliser without losing track of the set being acted on. Exam use: Action law, point, stabiliser calculation, orbit index and partition/Burnside check are shown.

practice.title: Practice 1 — orbit-stabiliser for the square action [9 marks]
practice.prompt: Let D 4 act on a square’s vertices. Find a vertex stabiliser and use orbit-stabiliser to calculate its orbit.
practice.route: Identify actual symmetries before substituting cardinalities. Fastest route. List identity and the reflection through the selected vertex/opposite vertex, then use |G|=|Orb(v)||Stab(v)|. Topic-specific trap. D 4 here has eight symmetries, not four. List identity and the reflection through the selected vertex/opposite vertex, then use |G|=|Orb(v)||Stab(v)|. Topic-specific trap. D 4 here has eight symmetries, not four. D 4 here has eight symmetries, not four.
practice.answer: Let D4 act on the four vertices of a square. For a vertex v, the stabiliser contains identity and the reflection through v and the opposite vertex, so has size 2. Since |D4|=8, orbit-stabiliser gives |Orb(v)|=8/2=4, as expected. For the action on diagonals, rotations by 0 and 180 fix both diagonals while 90 and 270 swap them; reflection counts depend on axis and can feed Burnside.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Let C 4 rotate the vertices of a square. Find the orbit and stabiliser of one vertex. Check: orbit size 4; stabiliser is trivial.
practice.route: 2. Prove a faithful action of G on n points gives G≤S n . Check: use the action homomorphism and trivial kernel.
practice.answer: 2. Prove a faithful action of G on n points gives G≤S n . Check: use the action homomorphism and trivial kernel.

practice.title: Practice 2 — Burnside count of binary necklaces [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Count length-four binary necklaces up to rotation.
practice.route: Burnside requires fixed-string counts for each rotation before averaging. Fastest route. Use fixed counts 16,2,4,2 for rotations by 0,1,2,3 positions. Topic-specific trap. Dividing 16 by four misses strings with nontrivial rotational symmetry. Use fixed counts 16,2,4,2 for rotations by 0,1,2,3 positions. Topic-specific trap. Dividing 16 by four misses strings with nontrivial rotational symmetry. Dividing 16 by four misses strings with nontrivial rotational symmetry.
practice.answer: use Burnside to count binary necklaces of length 4 under rotations. Check fixed strings for rotations 0,1,2,3 are 16,2,4,2, so orbits=(16+2+4+2)/4=6.

mistakes: Using orbit-stabiliser before checking the action.
Calling an action faithful when a nonidentity element fixes all points.
Confusing a point stabiliser with the kernel.
Recovery rule: The stabiliser is a subgroup of G, while the orbit is a subset of X; do not multiply their sets or swap their sizes.

sheets.title: Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms
sheets.purpose: Recognise maps, calculate kernel/image, and invoke the first isomorphism theorem with the correct quotient. Exam use: Well-definedness, operation law, kernel, image, normality and quotient/image orders are all checked.

practice.title: Practice 1 — kernel and image of a quotient-group homomorphism [9 marks]
practice.prompt: For φ:Z 12 →Z 8 , [x]↦[2x], prove well-definedness and find kernel, image and the first-isomorphism conclusion.
practice.route: Definition on representatives must be checked before using kernel algebra. Fastest route. Test x→x+12, solve 2x≡0 (mod 8), then list even residue classes. Topic-specific trap. A formula that looks homomorphic can still fail to be well-defined on residue classes. Test x→x+12, solve 2x≡0 (mod 8), then list even residue classes. Topic-specific trap. A formula that looks homomorphic can still fail to be well-defined on residue classes. A formula that looks homomorphic can still fail to be well-defined on residue classes.
practice.answer: Worked answer. Define φ:Z 12 →Z 8 by φ([x] 12 )=[2x] 8 . It is well-defined: replacing x by x+12k changes 2x by 24k, which is divisible by 8, so the output class is unchanged. It is a homomorphism because φ([x+y])=[2x+2y]=φ([x])+φ([y]). Its kernel consists of [x] 12 such that 2x≡0 (mod 8), equivalently x≡0 (mod 4), namely {[0],[4],[8]}. Its image is { [0],[2],[4],[6] }=2Z 8 . Hence the First Isomorphism Theorem gives Z 12 /ker φ≅2Z 8 , both groups having order 4.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Find ker and image of φ:Z 12 →Z 4 , [x]↦[x]. Check: image is all of Z 4 ; kernel has three elements.
practice.route: 2. If φ:G→H is a homomorphism of finite groups with |G|=60 and |kerφ|=5, find |imφ| and justify it. Check: 12, by the homomorphism counting formula.
practice.answer: 2. If φ:G→H is a homomorphism of finite groups with |G|=60 and |kerφ|=5, find |imφ| and justify it. Check: 12, by the homomorphism counting formula.

practice.title: Practice 2 — reject a non-well-defined residue formula [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Decide whether [x] 12 ↦[3x] 8 is well-defined.
practice.route: One pair of equal input classes with unequal images is decisive. Fastest route. Compare representatives 0 and 12. Topic-specific trap. Checking only additivity of the integer formula does not establish a map from Z 12 . Compare representatives 0 and 12. Topic-specific trap. Checking only additivity of the integer formula does not establish a map from Z 12 . Checking only additivity of the integer formula does not establish a map from Z 12 .
practice.answer: decide whether [x]12 -> [3x]8 is well-defined. Check changing by 12 changes output by 36, not divisible by 8, so it is not; test [0]=[12] gives 0 versus 4.

mistakes: Writing G/kerφ≅H without proving surjectivity.
Forgetting kernels are subsets of the domain.
Using additive notation on one side and multiplicative notation inconsistently.
Recovery rule: For maps on residue classes, well-definedness comes before homomorphism properties.

sheets.title: Lower-Frequency and Current-Scope Topics
sheets.purpose: Maintain a compact safety net for direct products, automorphisms, automata/regular languages and combinatorial actions. Exam use: Named theorem, normality, intersection, product size, action/factors and isomorphism conclusion are justified.

practice.title: Practice 1 — semidirect but not direct product in S 3 [9 marks]
practice.prompt: Show S 3 =A 3 H for H=⟨(12)⟩ and decide whether this is direct or semidirect.
practice.route: Verify orders, intersection and normality separately. Fastest route. Use |A 3 H|=|A 3 ||H|/|A 3 ∩H|, then test H. Topic-specific trap. One normal factor supports a semidirect product; direct product needs the appropriate commuting/normal structure. Use |A 3 H|=|A 3 ||H|/|A 3 ∩H|, then test H. Topic-specific trap. One normal factor supports a semidirect product; direct product needs the appropriate commuting/normal structure. One normal factor supports a semidirect product; direct product needs the appropriate commuting/normal structure.
practice.answer: In S3, A3 is normal of order 3 and H=< (12) > has order 2, A3 intersect H={e}, and |A3 H|=3*2=6, so S3=A3 H. Since H is not normal, this is not a direct product; it is A3 semidirect H, isomorphic to Z3 semidirect Z2 with inversion action.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Describe the language accepted by a two-state automaton that toggles state on each a and accepts the start state. Check: words with an even number of a's (assuming no other transitions change state).
practice.route: 2. State Burnside's lemma and list the data needed to count vertex colourings up to a symmetry group. Check: sum fixed colourings over group elements, divide by |G|.
practice.answer: 2. State Burnside's lemma and list the data needed to count vertex colourings up to a symmetry group. Check: sum fixed colourings over group elements, divide by |G|.

practice.title: Practice 2 — composition series of S 3 [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Give a composition series for S 3 and explain why its factors do not make S 3 ≅Z 6 .
practice.route: Name the normal inclusions and prove both factor groups simple. Fastest route. Use {e}<A 3 <S 3 with factors Z 3 , Z 2 . Topic-specific trap. Composition factors determine a multiset, not necessarily the group’s direct-product structure. Use {e}<A 3 <S 3 with factors Z 3 , Z 2 . Topic-specific trap. Composition factors determine a multiset, not necessarily the group’s direct-product structure. Composition factors determine a multiset, not necessarily the group’s direct-product structure.
practice.answer: give a composition series for S3. Check {e}<A3<S3 has factors A3/{e}=Z3 and S3/A3=Z2, both simple; explain why the nonabelian group is not their direct product Z6.

mistakes: Treating older-paper occurrence as a forecast.
Using Burnside without specifying the action and fixed set.
Giving an automaton answer without defining acceptance.
Recovery rule: Coprime subgroup orders and full product size do not by themselves give a direct product; both factors must be normal.

sheets.title: Simple Groups and Non-Simplicity
sheets.purpose: Build short, complete proofs that a finite group cannot be simple. Exam use: Candidate normal subgroup, all Sylow possibilities, intersection/count or action kernel, and proper/nontrivial conclusion are explicit.

practice.title: Practice 1 — Sylow counting excludes simplicity at order 30 [10 marks]
practice.prompt: Prove that no group of order 30 is simple.
practice.route: The non-uniqueness cases must be eliminated by a disjoint element count. Fastest route. List possible n 5 , n 3 , count nonidentity elements in distinct Sylow subgroups, and compare with 30. Topic-specific trap. Distinct prime-order Sylow subgroups intersect only in identity; do not double-count it. List possible n 5 , n 3 , count nonidentity elements in distinct Sylow subgroups, and compare with 30. Topic-specific trap. Distinct prime-order Sylow subgroups intersect only in identity; do not double-count it. Distinct prime-order Sylow subgroups intersect only in identity; do not double-count it.
practice.answer: No group G of order 30 is simple. Sylow gives n5 divides 6 and n5=1 mod 5, so n5=1 or 6; n3 divides 10 and n3=1 mod 3, so n3=1 or 10. If neither is 1, distinct Sylow subgroups contribute 6*4=24 elements of order 5 and 10*2=20 of order 3, disjoint except identity, exceeding 30. Hence one Sylow subgroup is normal.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. Prove a group with nontrivial proper centre is not simple. Check: Z(G) is normal.
practice.route: 2. Show no group of order 45 is simple. Check: use n 5 divides 9 and is 1 mod 5.
practice.answer: 2. Show no group of order 45 is simple. Check: use n 5 divides 9 and is 1 mod 5.

practice.title: Practice 2 — order 56 and the Sylow-7 action [9 marks]
practice.prompt: Investigate simplicity of a group of order 56 by its action on Sylow 7-subgroups.
practice.route: If n 7 =8, the induced action needs a kernel argument; an embedding claim alone is insufficient. Fastest route. First use n 7 ∣8 and n 7 ≡1 mod 7, then analyse the conjugation action. Topic-specific trap. A homomorphism G→S 8 does not automatically contradict |G|=56. First use n 7 ∣8 and n 7 ≡1 mod 7, then analyse the conjugation action. Topic-specific trap. A homomorphism G→S 8 does not automatically contradict |G|=56. A homomorphism G→S 8 does not automatically contradict |G|=56.
practice.answer: Worked answer. Let G have order 56=2 3 ·7. Sylow gives n 7 ∣8 and n 7 ≡1 (mod 7), hence n 7 =1 or 8. If n 7 =1, the unique Sylow 7-subgroup is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup and G is not simple. Suppose n 7 =8. Conjugation on the eight Sylow 7-subgroups gives a nontrivial homomorphism φ:G→S 8 ; its kernel is normal. If ker φ is nontrivial, it is proper because the action is nontrivial, so again G is not simple. If ker φ=1, the action is faithful, but that fact alone is not a contradiction. Instead count the Sylow subgroups: distinct subgroups of order 7 intersect only in the identity, so the eight of them contribute 8(7−1)=48 distinct nonidentity elements. There are therefore exactly 56−1−48=7 nonidentity elements left. Let Q be a Sylow 2-subgroup. It has order 8, hence seven nonidentity elements; none can lie in a subgroup of order 7. Thus Q consists of the identity together with exactly those seven remaining elements. Every Sylow 2-subgroup has the same seven nonidentity elements, so Q is unique. Therefore Q is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup. In all cases G is not simple.

mistakes: Finding a subgroup but never proving normality.
Calling G itself a witness to non-simplicity.
Stopping at a possible Sylow count rather than resolving it.
Recovery rule: Counting nonidentity elements from different Sylow p-subgroups is safe because their intersection is trivial; state that reason.

sheets.title: Subgroups and Lagrange's Theorem
sheets.purpose: Use subgroup tests and Lagrange's theorem efficiently in the recurring finite-group proof style. Exam use: Operation, nonempty/subgroup test, sizes, index/cosets and the exact divisibility implication are shown.

practice.title: Practice 1 — subgroup and cosets in Z 12 [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Show H={0,4,8} is a subgroup of additive Z 12 , and find its order, index, cosets and the order of 4.
practice.route: Give a subgroup proof before numerical conclusions. Fastest route. Use the one-step difference test, then list representatives 0,1,2,3. Topic-specific trap. In additive notation use a−b, not an unadapted multiplicative inverse argument. Use the one-step difference test, then list representatives 0,1,2,3. Topic-specific trap. In additive notation use a−b, not an unadapted multiplicative inverse argument. In additive notation use a−b, not an unadapted multiplicative inverse argument.
practice.answer: In Z12 under addition, H={0,4,8}. It is nonempty and for a,b in H, a-b is again a multiple of 4 mod 12, so H<=Z12. Its order is 3 and index 4. The cosets are H,1+H,2+H,3+H. Element 4 has order 3 since 3*4=0 mod 12 and no smaller positive multiple vanishes.

practice.title: Graduated exam bridge
practice.prompt: 1. If |G|=42, list possible orders of an element. Check: positive divisors of 42 only.
practice.route: 2. Let H={[[1,n],[0,1]]:n∈Z}. Prove H≤SL(2,Z) and show H≅Z. Check: multiply matrices to add parameters; n↦matrix(n) is an isomorphism.
practice.answer: 2. Let H={[[1,n],[0,1]]:n∈Z}. Prove H≤SL(2,Z) and show H≅Z. Check: multiply matrices to add parameters; n↦matrix(n) is an isomorphism.

practice.title: Practice 2 — a point stabiliser in S 4 [8 marks]
practice.prompt: Prove K={σ∈S 4 :σ(4)=4} is a subgroup and find its order and index.
practice.route: Link the stabiliser condition to closure and then to S 3 . Fastest route. Use ab⁻¹ fixing 4 and restrict permutations to {1,2,3}. Topic-specific trap. Fixing one point leaves 3!, not 4!, permissible permutations. Use ab⁻¹ fixing 4 and restrict permutations to {1,2,3}. Topic-specific trap. Fixing one point leaves 3!, not 4!, permissible permutations. Fixing one point leaves 3!, not 4!, permissible permutations.
practice.answer: show K={sigma in S4:sigma(4)=4} is a subgroup and find its order/index. Check ab^{-1} fixes 4 when a,b do; restriction to {1,2,3} gives K isomorphic to S3, so |K|=6 and index 4.

mistakes: Claiming every divisor of |G| is realised as an element order.
Using Lagrange before establishing subgroup status.
Confusing the order of G, H and an element.
Recovery rule: Lagrange says subgroup order must divide group order, not that every divisor occurs as a subgroup order.

sheets.title: Sylow Theorems
sheets.purpose: Apply the three Sylow theorems and turn congruence/divisibility into structural conclusions. Exam use: Full p-power, divisibility, congruence, complete candidate list, any intersection count and justified normality are explicit.

practice.title: Practice 1 — prove order 132 cannot be simple [10 marks]
practice.prompt: Use Sylow-number restrictions and an element count to prove every group of order 132 has a proper normal subgroup.
practice.route: The two possible unique Sylow subgroups must be reached by contradiction. Fastest route. List allowed n 11 , n 3 ; if neither is one, count the nonidentity elements contributed. practice.answer: Prove a group G of order 132=2^2*3*11 is not simple. Here n11 divides 12 and n11=1 mod 11, so n11=1 or 12; n3 divides 44 and n3=1 mod 3, so n3=1,4 or 22. If neither Sylow subgroup were unique, the 12 Sylow 11-subgroups would contribute 12*(11-1)=120 nonidentity elements and the 22 Sylow 3-subgroups would contribute 22*(3-1)=44. Subgroups of different prime orders intersect only in the identity, so this would require 164 distinct nonidentity elements in a group with only 131. Hence n11=1 or n3=1, giving a proper nontrivial normal subgroup.

mistakes: Using n p ≡0 mod p instead of 1.
Forgetting to divide |G| by the full p-power first.
Assuming all p-subgroups are Sylow p-subgroups.
Recovery rule: A candidate list with more than one value is not a conclusion; continue with counting, actions or another prime instead of selecting 1 by preference.
